rationale: The entry's distinctive claim—that Shadow of Death is specifically the inverse outline/pattern of the Shadow of Christ (Christ's feasts/appointed way leading through death to life), i.e., the contrary pattern of sin/darkness/bondage whose wages end in the pit—does not emerge from the cited texts as their best explanation. The primary passages (Ps 23:4; 107:10, 14; Isa 9:2; Luke 1:78-79) are explained more directly and with fewer imported steps by the common reading of deathly gloom/mortal peril or spiritual darkness dispelled by light. Rom 6:23 and Phil 2:5-9 supply general death-as-wages and Christ's path through death but do not identify tsalmaveth as the structural inverse of a feast-defined Shadow of Christ. The chapter's redefinition of 'shadow' as protective outline supplies the method but does not make the glossary identification the superior account of the listed verses.
book_core_identification: Shadow of Death is the inverse/outline opposite of the Shadow of Christ (Christ's appointed times/feasts/way leading through death to life): the contrary pattern of sin, darkness, and bondage ending in the pit or grave.
book_secondary_elaborations: A shadow is an image, outline, or boundary of its subject.
The Shadow of Christ is defined in part by His appointed times, feasts, assemblies, and way of living.
unsupported_glossary_assertions: The Shadow of Death is the inverse of the Shadow of Life—the Shadow of Christ.
The Shadow of Christ is defined in part by His appointed times, feasts, assemblies, and way of living, which leads through death into eternal life.
The Shadow of Death is the contrary pattern of sin, darkness, and bondage, whose wages end in the pit or grave.
chapter_only_objections: Chapter-wide claim that 'shadow' uniformly means protective shelter/covering (wings, tree, rock, cloud, hand) rather than gloom, used to reverse Col 2:16-17 discharge of feasts.
Chapter application that feasts remain present-tense shadows of the still-approaching body of Christ and that standing in them is standing in Messiah's shade.
Chapter claim that even shadow of death is harmless outline testifying to morning/light behind it, as part of larger 'it is good to be in the shadow' thesis.
Heaven-and-hell chapter's broader annihilationist/second-death framework and rejection of intermediate conscious torment, used as background for 'pit or grave'.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In the cited texts, 'shadow of death' (tsalmaveth/skia thanatou) is a conventional poetic metaphor for deepest darkness, mortal peril, affliction, or the spiritual hopelessness of those sitting without God's light; God accompanies the believer through it or shines messianic light into it. It is not a technical inverse pattern opposite a feast-defined Shadow of Christ.
counter_core_identification: Deepest darkness/gloom of mortal danger, affliction, or spiritual lostness, through which God delivers or into which Christ's light shines.
material_core_denial: The phrase does not name a structural inverse of Christ's appointed times/feasts/way; it names the extremity of darkness or death-threat itself (or the condition of those dwelling in it).
counter_case: Ps 23:4 presents a valley walked through under God's rod/staff comfort—paradigmatic mortal peril or death-threat, not a sin-pattern inverse to feasts.
Ps 107:10, 14 pairs shadow of death with darkness, bondage, and affliction from which God frees prisoners—concrete deliverance language, not cosmic inverse of Shadow of Christ.
Isa 9:2 / Matt 4:16 / Luke 1:78-79 use the phrase for people dwelling/sitting in darkness who receive light; the contrast is light vs. darkness, not feast-pattern vs. sin-pattern.
Job, Jeremiah, and Amos usages (background to the idiom) repeatedly mean thick gloom, the grave's darkness, or calamity without requiring an inverse-to-Christ structure.
Rom 6:23 states wages of sin = death vs. gift of life, and Phil 2 narrates Christ's obedience unto death then exaltation; neither text equates tsalmaveth with the contrary of a feast-shadow.
Modern lexical alternative (tsalmut = deep darkness) and traditional LXX/Vulgate 'shadow of death' both fit the peril/darkness reading without the entry's system.
book_explanatory_advantages: Unifies 'shadow' vocabulary via tsel/tselem (outline/image) and notes that a shadow implies a body and light.
Links Rom 6:23 death-as-wages to the end-point 'pit or grave'.
Notes Christ's path through death (Phil 2) as the life-side counterpart.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for every primary citation with the texts' own parallel terms (darkness, valley, bondage, light shining) and no extra system of inverse shadows.
Fits the full range of OT poetic usage (Job, Psalms, Prophets) as extreme gloom/peril without forcing feast typology.
Explains NT reuse (Matt 4; Luke 1) as direct fulfillment of Isa 9 light-into-darkness without requiring Colossians feast machinery.
Requires no redefinition of the everyday metaphor; the comfort in Ps 23 and the light in Isa/Luke work immediately.
Accommodates both 'death-shadow' and 'deep-darkness' vocalizations equally well.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Ps 23:4's pastoral comfort ('I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me') while walking the valley—functions as presence-in-peril, not as diagnosis of an anti-feast sin pattern.
The consistent pairing of 'shadow of death' with 'darkness' and deliverance/light across Ps 107, Isa 9, and Luke 1, which never mentions appointed times, feasts, or an inverse Shadow of Christ.
Absence of any textual link in the cited verses between tsalmaveth and the Colossians/Hebrews 'shadow of things to come' feast language that the entry presupposes.
decisive_sources: Common lexical and traditional readings of tsalmaveth across Job/Psalms/Prophets
unresolved_objections: The chapter's broader redefinition of every 'shadow' as shelter/outline remains a coherent internal system even if it does not make the glossary entry the best reading of these particular verses.
Rom 6:23 and the pit/grave endpoint are compatible with both readings and do not decide between them.
